claims.claim: toiL acts as a sensor for translation stress caused by multiple classes of ribosome-targeting antibiotics.
claims.source: We further show that the long 5′ UR of topAI encodes a regulatory uORF, toiL (Figure 1A), that acts as a sensor for translation stress caused by multiple classes of ribosome-targeting antibiotics.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing antibiotic-induced expression.

claims.claim: Genome-scale analysis of Rho termination identified a putative termination site in the coding region of topAI.
claims.source: Genome-scale analysis of Rho termination identified a putative termination site in the coding region of topAI (Adams et al., 2021; Peters et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genome-scale studies.

claims.claim: The topAI transcript has an unusually long UR (171 nt).
claims.source: The topAI transcript has an unusually long UR (171 nt) (Thomason et al., 2015), suggesting that Rho termination within topAI may be regulated by sequences in the UR.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Thomason et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Rho termination within topAI may be regulated by sequences in the UR.
claims.source: The topAI transcript has an unusually long UR (171 nt) (Thomason et al., 2015), suggesting that Rho termination within topAI may be regulated by sequences in the UR.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of a long UR.

claims.claim: Expression of a topAI-lacZ transcriptional reporter fusion is approximately sevenfold higher in rho mutant cells than in wild-type cells.
claims.source: We observed approximately sevenfold higher expression in rho mutant cells than in wild-type cells (Figure 1C), consistent with a Rho termination site upstream of position 42 of the topAI gene.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: There is a Rho termination site upstream of position 42 of the topAI gene.
claims.source: We observed approximately sevenfold higher expression in rho mutant cells than in wild-type cells (Figure 1C), consistent with a Rho termination site upstream of position 42 of the topAI gene.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the reporter assay data showing increased expression in rho mutant.

claims.claim: Mutating four C residues in the pyrimidine-rich region at the 5' end of topAI caused a fourfold increase in expression in wild-type cells.
claims.source: Mutating just four C residues in the Rho-terminated construct of topAI (Figure 1B) caused a fourfold increase in expression in wild-type cells, but no change in expression in rho mutant cells (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Mutating four C residues in the pyrimidine-rich region at the 5' end of topAI caused no change in expression in rho mutant cells.
claims.source: Mutating just four C residues in the Rho-terminated construct of topAI (Figure 1B) caused a fourfold increase in expression in wild-type cells, but no change in expression in rho mutant cells (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The rut includes the pyrimidine-rich sequence at the very 5' end of the topAI transcript.
claims.source: We conclude that the rut includes the pyrimidine-rich sequence at the very 5' end of the topAI transcript.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mutational analysis data.

claims.claim: Most of the transcription termination occurs between nucleotides 10 and 42 of the topAI coding region.
claims.source: This suggests that most of the transcription termination occurs between nucleotides 10 and 42 of the topAI coding region.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from comparing reporter constructs of different lengths.

claims.claim: Rho loads onto the RNA early in the topAI transcript, but does not trigger termination until RNAP is within the ORF, >180 nt further downstream.
claims.source: We conclude that Rho loads onto the RNA early in the topAI transcript, but does not trigger termination until RNAP is within the ORF, >180 nt further downstream.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the location of the rut and the termination site.

claims.claim: Translating ribosomes protect nascent mRNA in protein-coding regions from Rho.
claims.source: Translating ribosomes protect nascent mRNA in protein-coding regions from Rho (de Smit et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (de Smit et al., 2009).

claims.claim: topAI is translationally repressed.
claims.source: Given that Rho termination occurs within the topAI ORF, we speculated that topAI is translationally repressed.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from translational reporter assays.

claims.claim: Strong repression of the topAI-lux translation is observed in both wild-type and rho mutant cells.
claims.source: Although transcriptional repression of topAI is relieved in the rho mutant background (Figure 1), we observed strong repression of the topAI-lux translation in both wild-type and rho mutant cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Rho termination within the topAI coding region is a consequence of translational repression.
claims.source: These data suggest that Rho termination within the topAI coding region is a consequence of translational repression.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that translation is repressed even when Rho termination is relieved.

claims.claim: Long 5′ URs often contain regulatory elements such as uORFs that contribute to regulation of the downstream genes.
claims.source: Long 5′ URs often contain regulatory elements such as uORFs that contribute to regulation of the downstream genes (Kriner et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Kriner et al., 2016).

claims.claim: An eight-codon putative uORF starts 139 nt upstream of topAI.
claims.source: Through manual inspection of available ribosome profiling data, we identified an eight-codon putative uORF that starts 139 nt upstream of topAI (Figure 4A; Meydan et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2015; Weaver et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of published ribosome profiling data and shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: A small protein (Mia-127) with near-identical amino acid sequence and relative genome position was described in Salmonella enterica.
claims.source: A small protein (Mia-127) with near-identical amino acid sequence and relative genome position was described in Salmonella enterica (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Baek et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Baek et al., 2017) and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Replacing native codons with stop codons in the predicted CDS prevented expression of the toiL-lacZ fusion.
claims.source: Replacing native codons with stop codons in the predicted CDS prevented expression of this fusion, unlike the equivalent substitution upstream of the ORF (Figure 4), supporting our ORF prediction.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The first seven amino acids of the ToiL protein are conserved across bacteria that encode the topAI-yjhQP operon.
claims.source: The first seven amino acids of the ToiL protein are conserved across bacteria that encode the topAI-yjhQP operon (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The toiL start codon mutation caused a 12- to 110-fold decrease in topAI induction by antibiotics.
claims.source: The toiL start codon mutation caused a 12- to 110-fold decrease in topAI induction by antibiotics (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Disruption of the toiL S-D site abolished induction of topAI expression by all antibiotics tested.
claims.source: Disruption of the toiL S-D site abolished induction of topAI expression by all antibiotics tested (Figure 5B), supporting the idea that active translation of toiL is absolutely required for topAI regulation by ribosome-targeting antibiotics.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Active translation of toiL is absolutely required for topAI regulation by ribosome-targeting antibiotics.
claims.source: Disruption of the toiL S-D site abolished induction of topAI expression by all antibiotics tested (Figure 5B), supporting the idea that active translation of toiL is absolutely required for topAI regulation by ribosome-targeting antibiotics.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the S-D mutation data.

claims.claim: Supplying the mutant 23S rRNA (ΔT1917) in trans resulted in increased topAI expression.
claims.source: Supplying the mutant 23S rRNA in trans resulted in increased topAI expression, whereas wild-type 23S rRNA did not (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Wild-type 23S rRNA supplied in trans did not result in increased topAI expression.
claims.source: Supplying the mutant 23S rRNA in trans resulted in increased topAI expression, whereas wild-type 23S rRNA did not (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The 23S rRNA mutation is dominant over the seven chromosomal rRNA operons.
claims.source: Thus, the 23S rRNA mutation is dominant over the seven chromosomal rRNA operons, suggesting that the effect of the mutations in 23S rRNA genes on topAI expression is not simply due to a reduction in the levels of active ribosomes.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that a single mutant rRNA operon in trans can induce topAI expression.

claims.claim: Expression of toxin–antitoxin genes is often induced by environmental stresses.
claims.source: Expression of toxin–antitoxin genes is often induced by environmental stresses (Page and Peti, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a review (Page and Peti, 2016).

claims.claim: Increases in topAI mRNA levels upon treatment with erythromycin or clindamycin have been reported previously.
claims.source: Moreover, increases in topAI mRNA levels upon treatment with erythromycin or clindamycin have been reported previously (Dzyubak and Yap, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Dzyubak and Yap, 2016).

claims.claim: Tetracycline, spectinomycin, retapamulin, tylosin, and erythromycin caused increases in expression from 250-fold to 4000-fold of the topAI-lux translational fusion.
claims.source: Tetracycline, spectinomycin, retapamulin, tylosin, and erythromycin caused increases in expression from 250-fold to 4000-fold of the topAI-lux translational fusion (Figure 2C; Supplementary file 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Supplementary file 1B.

claims.claim: No change in topAI expression was observed in response to treatment with chloramphenicol.
claims.source: We observed no change in expression in response to treatment with chloramphenicol (Figure 2C), kasugamycin, gentamicin, amikacin, streptomycin, apramycin, or hygromycin (Supplementary file 1B), although we cannot rule out that these antibiotics might induce topAI expression at concentrations other than those tested here.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: topAI RNA levels are strongly increased upon treatment with gentamicin.
claims.source: Indeed, a previous study showed that topAI RNA levels are strongly increased upon treatment with gentamicin (Kohanski et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Kohanski et al., 2008).

claims.claim: topAI levels are strongly induced upon treatment with kanamycin.
claims.source: Another study showed that topAI levels are strongly induced upon treatment with kanamycin (Shaw et al., 2003), an antibiotic not tested in our work.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Shaw et al., 2003).

claims.claim: topAI expression is modulated by a wide variety of mechanistically distinct ribosome-targeting antibiotics.
claims.source: In summary, topAI expression is modulated by a wide variety of mechanistically distinct ribosome-targeting antibiotics, reinforcing the idea that expression of this toxin–antitoxin system responds to the translation status of the cell.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the antibiotic induction data.

claims.claim: Expression of the topAI-yjhQP toxin–antitoxin system responds to the translation status of the cell.
claims.source: In summary, topAI expression is modulated by a wide variety of mechanistically distinct ribosome-targeting antibiotics, reinforcing the idea that expression of this toxin–antitoxin system responds to the translation status of the cell.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that multiple translation-targeting antibiotics induce topAI.

claims.claim: Mutation of rho led to a significant 12.0-fold increase in RNAP occupancy within rho.
claims.source: Mutation of rho led to a significant 12.0-fold increase in RNAP occupancy within rho (t-test p=0.001), consistent with Rho-dependent transcription termination early in the rho transcript (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Tetracycline treatment in wild-type cells did not lead to a significant increase in RNAP occupancy within rho.
claims.source: Tetracycline treatment in wild-type cells did not lead to a significant increase in RNAP occupancy within rho (t-test p=0.1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data.

claims.claim: The combination of mutating rho and treating with tetracycline led to a significant 5.9-fold increase in RNAP occupancy within rho.
claims.source: The combination of mutating rho and treating with tetracycline led to a significant 5.9-fold increase in RNAP occupancy within rho (t-test p=0.0009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data.

claims.claim: Mutation of rho led to significant 3.6-, 18.9-, and 17.8-fold increases in RNAP occupancy at three positions across the topAI-yjhQP operon.
claims.source: Mutation of rho led to significant 3.6-, 18.9-, and 17.8-fold increases in RNAP occupancy at three positions across the topAI-yjhQP operon (Figure 3C; t-test p=0.009, 0.004, and 0.001, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Tetracycline treatment in wild-type cells led to significant 1.7-, 7.3-, and 6.7-fold increases in RNAP occupancy at the three positions across the topAI-yjhQP operon.
claims.source: Tetracycline treatment in wild-type cells led to significant 1.7-, 7.3-, and 6.7-fold increases in RNAP occupancy at the three positions across the topAI-yjhQP operon (t-test p=0.03, 0.0009, and 0.001, respectively), consistent with tetracycline treatment inhibiting Rho-dependent transcription termination within topAI.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data.

claims.claim: Tetracycline treatment inhibits Rho-dependent transcription termination within topAI.
claims.source: Tetracycline treatment in wild-type cells led to significant 1.7-, 7.3-, and 6.7-fold increases in RNAP occupancy at the three positions across the topAI-yjhQP operon (t-test p=0.03, 0.0009, and 0.001, respectively), consistent with tetracycline treatment inhibiting Rho-dependent transcription termination within topAI.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ChIP-qPCR data showing increased RNAP occupancy.

claims.claim: Mutation of rho led to significant 7.5-, 5-, and 8.4-fold increases in RNA levels at three positions across the topAI-yjhQP operon.
claims.source: Mutation of rho led to significant 7.5-, 5-, and 8.4-fold increases in RNA levels at three positions across the topAI-yjhQP operon (Figure 3D; t-test p=0.002, 0.002, and 3.5e–7, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Premature Rho-dependent transcription termination destabilizes the topAI-yjhQP mRNA.
claims.source: Given that the most upstream region tested is upstream of the likely Rho termination site, these data suggest that premature Rho-dependent transcription termination destabilizes the topAI-yjhQP mRNA.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RNA levels increase even upstream of the termination site when Rho is mutated.

claims.claim: Tetracycline treatment in wild-type cells led to significant 4.9-, 2.0-, and 8.0-fold increases in RNA levels at the three positions across the topAI-yjhQP operon.
claims.source: Tetracycline treatment in wild-type cells led to significant 4.9-, 2.0-, and 8.0-fold increases in RNA levels at the three positions across the topAI-yjhQP operon (t-test p=0.008, 0.0007, and 8.2e–6, respectively), consistent with tetracycline treatment inhibiting Rho-dependent transcription termination within topAI.
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data.

claims.claim: Tetracycline treatment induces translation of topAI, which in turn prevents premature Rho-dependent transcription termination within topAI.
claims.source: Together, our data support a model in which tetracycline treatment induces translation of topAI, which in turn prevents premature Rho-dependent transcription termination within topAI.
claims.evidence: This is a model based on the combined ChIP-qPCR and qRT-PCR data.

claims.claim: Computational prediction of the topAI UR RNA secondary structure suggests that sequences within toiL base-pair with the topAI ribosome-binding site.
claims.source: Computational prediction of the topAI UR RNA secondary structure suggests that sequences within toiL base-pair with the topAI ribosome-binding site (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is based on computational RNA structure prediction shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The 5' UR of toiL has been reported to form an extended region of dsRNA.
claims.source: Consistent with this prediction, the 5' UR of toiL has been reported to form an extended region of dsRNA (Lybecker et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Lybecker et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Base-pairing between toiL and the topAI ribosome-binding site is supported by a structural prediction that incorporates sequence conservation information from orthologous regions in related species.
claims.source: Base-pairing between toiL and the topAI ribosome-binding site is further supported by a structural prediction that incorporates sequence conservation information from orthologous regions in related species (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on PETfold analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The SHAPE-seq data for untreated cells were in good agreement with the computationally predicted structure of the topAI UR.
claims.source: The SHAPE-seq data for untreated cells were in good agreement with the computationally predicted structure of the topAI UR (Figure 6A; Supplementary file 1C): the beginning of the 5' mRNA end is highly reactive, as are predicted loops.
claims.evidence: This is supported by SHAPE-seq experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Tetracycline treatment significantly altered reactivity in two distinct regions in the 5′ region: sequence from the toiL S-D to the toiL start codon became less reactive, whereas the topAI S-D became more reactive.
claims.source: Tetracycline treatment significantly altered reactivity (p<0.05; see 'Materials and methods' for details) in two distinct regions in the 5′ region in comparison to the untreated control: sequence from the toiL S-D to the toiL start codon became less reactive, whereas the topAI S-D became more reactive (Figure 6B; Supplementary file 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by SHAPE-seq experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: In the presence of tetracycline, initiating ribosomes stall at the start of toiL, which leads to a decrease in base-pairing between toiL and the topAI S-D.
claims.source: We propose that, in the presence of tetracycline, initiating ribosomes stall at the start of toiL, which leads to a decrease in base-pairing between toiL and the topAI S-D.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the SHAPE-seq data showing changes in reactivity.

claims.claim: topAI and its operonic genes yjhQ and yjhP are among the most strongly induced by tetracycline.
claims.source: A comparison of ribosome occupancy across all genes showed that topAI and its operonic genes yjhQ and yjhP are among the most strongly induced by tetracycline (Figure 7A; Supplementary file 1D; note that induction could be at the level of RNA abundance, translation, or both).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: For cells treated with tetracycline, ribosome occupancy throughout toiL was substantially higher than in untreated cells.
claims.source: For cells treated with tetracycline, ribosome occupancy throughout toiL was substantially higher than in untreated cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data.

claims.claim: A strong peak at position +18 of toiL is consistent with the downstream edge of a ribosome stalled at the toiL start codon.
claims.source: When mapping the 3' ends of ribosome-protected RNA fragments, we observed a strong peak at position +18 of toiL, a location consistent with the downstream edge of a ribosome stalled at the toiL start codon (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Tetracycline induced stalling at positions +16 to +18 relative to start codons.
claims.source: Tetracycline induced stalling at positions +16 to +18 relative to start codons (Figure 7C), consistent with ribosomes stalled at start codons, as has been described for tetracycline in an earlier study (Nakahigashi et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 7C and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Tetracycline induces expression of topAI by stalling ribosomes at the start codon of toiL.
claims.source: We conclude that tetracycline induces expression of topAI by stalling ribosomes at the start codon of toiL.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ribosome profiling data.

claims.claim: Retapamulin is a ribosome-targeting antibiotic that traps initiating ribosomes on start codons.
claims.source: We reasoned that retapamulin, a ribosome-targeting antibiotic that traps initiating ribosomes on start codons (Meydan et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2006), would induce topAI expression by the same mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Meydan et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2006).

claims.claim: Retapamulin strongly induced (~600-fold) expression of the topAI-lux translational reporter fusion.
claims.source: Consistent with this prediction, retapamulin strongly induced (~600-fold) expression of the topAI-lux translational reporter fusion (Figure 2C), and induction by retapamulin depended upon active translation of toiL (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Induction by retapamulin depended upon active translation of toiL.
claims.source: Consistent with this prediction, retapamulin strongly induced (~600-fold) expression of the topAI-lux translational reporter fusion (Figure 2C), and induction by retapamulin depended upon active translation of toiL (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Tetracycline and retapamulin induced expression most strongly with the fusion to the start codon of toiL.
claims.source: Tetracycline and retapamulin induced expression most strongly with the fusion to the start codon of toiL (Figure 8C), consistent with ribosome stalling at the start codon.
claims.evidence: This is supported by stalling reporter assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Tylosin induced expression of only the 5-codon fusion reporter construct, suggesting tylosin-induced stalling at Val5.
claims.source: Tylosin induced expression of only the 5-codon fusion reporter construct, suggesting tylosin-induced stalling at Val5.
claims.evidence: This is supported by stalling reporter assay data and is an inference about the stalling position.

claims.claim: The effect of tylosin on expression of the 5-codon reporter was abolished by the Val5→Leu mutation.
claims.source: The effect of tylosin on expression of this reporter was abolished by the Val5→Leu mutation (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by stalling reporter assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Erythromycin induced expression most strongly with the construct that has the complete toiL ORF, including the stop codon, suggesting that ribosomes stall during translation termination.
claims.source: Erythromycin induced expression most strongly with the construct that has the complete toiL ORF, including the stop codon (Figure 8C), suggesting that ribosomes stall during translation termination.
claims.evidence: This is supported by stalling reporter assay data shown in Figure 8C and is an inference about the stalling position.

claims.claim: Spectinomycin induced expression of several constructs, but the level of induction was lower than for other antibiotics.
claims.source: Spectinomycin induced expression of several constructs, but the level of induction was lower than for other antibiotics (Figure 8C), despite being able to induce topAI to a similar extent to tetracycline (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by stalling reporter assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Chloramphenicol did not induce expression of any of the stalling reporter constructs.
claims.source: Chloramphenicol did not induce expression of any of the constructs, consistent with its inability to induce expression of topAI (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by stalling reporter assay data.

claims.claim: A variety of ribosome-targeting antibiotics cause ribosomes to stall within toiL, with different antibiotics stalling ribosomes at different positions.
claims.source: Overall, these data suggest that a variety of ribosome-targeting antibiotics cause ribosomes to stall within toiL, with different antibiotics stalling ribosomes at different positions.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the stalling reporter assay data.

claims.claim: Ribosome stalling at a variety of positions within toiL is sufficient to induce topAI-yjhQP expression.
claims.source: Moreover, the data suggest that ribosome stalling at a variety of positions within toiL is sufficient to induce topAI-yjhQP expression.

results.result: The topAI-yjhQP operon is regulated by an 8-codon upstream ORF (uORF) named toiL, located 139 nt upstream of topAI. This uORF is conserved across related bacterial species and acts as a sensor for translation stress caused by multiple classes of ribosome-targeting antibiotics.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C32, C49, C51, and C52 provide converging experimental evidence from ribosome profiling, reporter assays, and sequence conservation analysis. The identification of toiL through manual inspection of ribosome profiling data (C49), validation through stop codon insertion experiments (C51), and demonstration of sequence conservation (C52) provide strong support for this result.

results.result: Rho-dependent transcription termination occurs within the topAI coding region (between nucleotides 10-42) as a consequence of translational repression. The Rho utilization (Rut) site is located in the 5' UR at the pyrimidine-rich sequence, and Rho loads early but terminates >180 nt downstream within the ORF.
results.evaluation: Multiple lines of experimental evidence support this result: reporter assays in rho mutants (C37, C39-40), ChIP-qPCR showing increased RNAP occupancy in rho mutants (C67, C70), and qRT-PCR showing increased RNA levels (C73). The mutational analysis of the Rut sequence (C39-41) and comparison of reporter constructs of different lengths (C42) provide strong mechanistic support.

results.result: Active translation of toiL is absolutely required for antibiotic-mediated induction of topAI expression. Five different classes of ribosome-targeting antibiotics (tetracycline, spectinomycin, retapamulin, tylosin, and erythromycin) induce topAI expression 250- to 4000-fold, while chloramphenicol and several aminoglycosides do not.
results.evaluation: The requirement for toiL translation is demonstrated by mutations in the toiL start codon (C53) and Shine-Dalgarno sequence (C54) that abolish or greatly reduce antibiotic induction. The luciferase reporter assays (C61) provide quantitative measurements of induction by multiple antibiotics with appropriate controls (C62), supporting the conclusion that topAI responds to diverse translation stresses.

results.result: In the absence of translation stress, a secondary structure in the 5' UR forms a hairpin between toiL and the topAI ribosome-binding site, occluding the topAI RBS and repressing translation. This structure is supported by computational predictions, prior dsRNA mapping, and SHAPE-seq data.
results.evaluation: The proposed RNA secondary structure is supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: computational prediction (C77), prior experimental dsRNA mapping (C78), evolutionary conservation analysis (C79), and in-cell SHAPE-seq data (C80-81). The SHAPE-seq experiments show statistically significant changes in reactivity upon tetracycline treatment consistent with the model (C81), providing strong experimental validation.

results.result: Different ribosome-targeting antibiotics stall ribosomes at different positions within toiL: tetracycline and retapamulin stall at the start codon (+16 to +18), tylosin stalls at Val5, and erythromycin stalls during translation termination. Ribosome stalling at any of these positions is sufficient to induce topAI expression.
results.evaluation: This result is supported by ribosome profiling data showing tetracycline-induced stalling at start codons genome-wide (C86) and specifically at toiL (C85), and by stalling reporter assays that map antibiotic-specific stalling positions (C91-95). The observation that different antibiotics induce expression despite stalling at different positions (C97-98) is well-supported by the experimental data, though the spectinomycin data are less clear (C95).

results.result: Tetracycline treatment relieves topAI repression by inducing ribosome stalling within toiL, which disrupts the repressive hairpin structure, leading to topAI translation. This translation in turn prevents premature Rho-dependent transcription termination within topAI.
results.evaluation: The model is supported by ChIP-qPCR showing tetracycline increases RNAP occupancy across topAI-yjhQP (C71), qRT-PCR showing increased RNA levels (C75), and the integration of structural, ribosome profiling, and reporter data. The mechanistic link between translation and Rho termination is well-established and the data are internally consistent.

results.result: Mutations in 23S rRNA (ΔT1917 in helix 69) induce topAI expression when supplied in trans, and this effect is dominant over the seven wild-type chromosomal rRNA operons, suggesting the effect is not simply due to reduced ribosome levels.
results.evaluation: The trans-complementation experiment (C56-57) with appropriate controls demonstrates that the mutant rRNA can induce topAI expression. The dominance observation (C58) is a reasonable inference from the data, though the mechanism by which a single mutant operon dominates is not fully explained. The result is consistent with the model that ribosome processivity defects can induce topAI.

results.result: toiL is a multipurpose uORF capable of responding to diverse translation stresses because base-pairing with the topAI ribosome-binding site occurs across the entire length of the toiL ORF, allowing ribosome stalling at any position within toiL to disrupt the repressive hairpin.
results.evaluation: This conclusion (C9, C106-107) is well-supported by the structural data showing extensive base-pairing (C77-79), the stalling reporter data showing that different antibiotics stall at different positions yet all induce expression (C91-98), and the observation that mutations at different positions in toiL affect regulation (C53-54). The mechanistic explanation is logical and consistent with all experimental observations.

results.result: In rho mutant cells, tetracycline treatment causes an additional ~2-fold increase in topAI-yjhQP RNA levels, suggesting a modest additional level of regulation at the level of mRNA stability.
results.evaluation: While the qRT-PCR data (C104) show a statistically significant 2-fold increase, the interpretation as mRNA stability regulation (C105) is speculative. The increase could also reflect transcriptional effects, RNA processing, or other mechanisms. Additional experiments such as RNA half-life measurements would be needed to definitively establish mRNA stability as the mechanism.

results.result: The mechanism by which translation prevents Rho termination at topAI is distinct from other characterized examples because the Rut is located in the 5' UR rather than within the ORF. Ribosomes translating topAI likely prevent Rho from catching elongating RNAP rather than preventing Rho loading, and the Rut must overlap the actively translated toiL ORF.
results.evaluation: The location of the Rut in the 5' UR (C139) is well-established by the mutational analysis (C39-41). The inference that this represents a distinct mechanism (C140-141) is logical given the unusual Rut location. The conclusion that the Rut overlaps toiL (C144-145) is a reasonable inference based on the length requirements for Rut sequences and the genomic organization.

results.result: Premature Rho-dependent transcription termination destabilizes the topAI-yjhQP mRNA, as evidenced by increased RNA levels even upstream of the termination site when Rho is mutated.
results.evaluation: The qRT-PCR data showing increased RNA levels upstream of the termination site in rho mutants (C73) support this inference (C74). The observation that RNA levels increase in regions that should not be directly affected by termination suggests a destabilization effect, though the mechanism is not fully elucidated.

results.result: Analysis of ribosome profiling data reveals that several other genes known to be associated with uORFs (mgtA, corA, speC) show >5-fold increases in ribosome-associated RNA levels upon tetracycline treatment, suggesting widespread uORF-mediated regulation in E. coli.
results.evaluation: The ribosome profiling analysis (C157) provides direct evidence for tetracycline-responsive regulation of other known uORF-containing genes. This supports the broader implication that uORF-mediated antibiotic sensing may be more widespread than previously recognized, though functional validation of these specific cases would strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: The mechanisms by which different antibiotics induce ribosome stalling within toiL are consistent with their known mechanisms of action and sequence preferences. Tetracycline likely prevents aminoacyl-tRNA association at the A-site of initiating ribosomes; macrolides (erythromycin, tylosin) induce stalling through nascent peptide-antibiotic interactions in the exit tunnel; and chloramphenicol fails to induce stalling due to the absence of its preferred codons (Ala, Ser, Thr) in toiL.
results.evaluation: The mechanistic explanations are well-supported by citations to prior work on antibiotic mechanisms (C120, C123-127, C130-131, C135) and are consistent with the experimental observations in this study. The comparison of toiL and msrDL sequences (C127-128) provides additional support for the erythromycin stalling mechanism. The chloramphenicol explanation (C136) is speculative but reasonable given the sequence composition of toiL.

results.result: Background on bacterial gene regulation: Expression of many bacterial genes is regulated by cis- and trans-acting elements in 5' URs, including uORFs that sense translation stress through ribosome stalling. Translation repression can lead to Rho-dependent transcription termination, and genome-wide studies suggest this is a widespread regulatory mechanism.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1-C26) represent established knowledge in the field, supported by appropriate citations to prior work. They provide necessary context for understanding the significance of the topAI regulatory mechanism but do not constitute novel findings of this study.

results.result: Background on the topAI-yjhQP system: The topAI gene is operonic with yjhQ and yjhP, encoding a type II toxin-antitoxin system. Previous genome-scale studies identified a Rho termination site in topAI, and prior studies reported induction by certain antibiotics.
results.evaluation: These claims (C27-C30, C34-C35, C59-C60, C63-C64) are supported by appropriate citations to prior work and provide necessary background for the current study. They establish what was known about the system before this work.

results.result: Comparison to other antibiotic-sensing uORFs: Several other bacterial uORFs (cplR, vmlR, vga(A), whiB7) sense multiple antibiotics, but most stall ribosomes at start codons. The toiL system is distinctive in that different antibiotics stall at different positions within the uORF.
results.evaluation: The comparisons to other systems (C111-C114, C116-C119) are supported by appropriate citations and accurately represent prior work. The distinction drawn between toiL and these other systems (C115) is well-supported by the experimental data in this study.

results.result: Two alternative mechanisms are proposed for how Rho can load onto the topAI 5' region despite the overlapping toiL ORF: (i) Rho loads only after toiL translation terminates, or (ii) Rho loops the RNA around toiL to access upstream and downstream Rut elements.
results.evaluation: These are speculative proposals (C146-C147) without direct experimental support in this study. While the citation to prior work on Rho stepping over roadblocks (C148) provides some precedent, neither proposed mechanism is tested experimentally. Additional experiments would be needed to distinguish between these possibilities.

results.result: Mutations in helix 69 and helix 80 of 23S rRNA induce topAI expression because these residues promote ribosome processivity, and slowed ribosomes translating toiL have effects similar to stalled ribosomes.
results.evaluation: This explanation (C108) is supported by citations to prior work on ribosome processivity and is consistent with the genetic screen results and the trans-complementation data (C56-C58). The mechanistic link between reduced processivity and the toiL regulatory mechanism is logical.

results.result: Speculation on physiological function and prevalence: The toiL sequence may have evolved to stall ribosomes in response to various antibiotics. The physiological signal that toiL senses could be antibiotics or non-antibiotic molecules like amino acids or polyamines. Large numbers of regulatory uORFs may exist even in well-characterized bacteria like E. coli.
results.evaluation: These are speculative claims (C110, C152-C153, C156) that extend beyond the experimental data. While the speculation is reasonable and supported by citations to related work, these hypotheses require additional experimental validation. The suggestion about widespread uORFs (C156) is supported by the ribosome profiling analysis (C157) but remains speculative.

results.result: The authors identify an 8-codon upstream ORF (uORF) named toiL located 139 nt upstream of topAI that acts as a regulatory sensor for translation stress caused by multiple classes of ribosome-targeting antibiotics. This uORF is conserved across related bacterial species and is supported by ribosome profiling data and sequence conservation analysis.
results.evaluation: All reviewers describe this as convincing evidence and a key discovery. The editor states the authors 'provide convincing evidence that translation of a short ORF denoted toiL...is responsive to different ribosome-targeting antibiotics.' Multiple reviewers affirm the identification and characterization of toiL without raising concerns about this finding.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that topAI is translationally repressed under normal conditions, and this translation repression leads to premature Rho-dependent transcription termination within the topAI ORF. The Rho utilization (Rut) site is located in the 5' upstream region, and termination occurs between nucleotides 10 and 42 of topAI.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently describe the model as 'appealing' and supported by 'convincing data.' One reviewer states 'the authors provide convincing data to support an elegant model in which ribosome stalling by ToiL promotes downstream topAI translation and prevents premature Rho-dependent transcription termination.' The experimental data from reporter assays and ChIP-qPCR are accepted without challenge.

results.result: Five different classes of ribosome-targeting antibiotics (tetracycline, spectinomycin, retapamulin, tylosin, and erythromycin) induce topAI expression by 250- to 4000-fold, while chloramphenicol and several aminoglycosides do not induce expression. This demonstrates that topAI expression responds to a wide variety of mechanistically distinct ribosome-targeting antibiotics.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without criticism. The editor notes the study uses 'a creative approach to map the different locations of ribosome stalling within toiL induced by different antibiotics.' One reviewer states the authors 'describe how translation of an 8-codon uORF denoted toiL...is responsive to different ribosome-targeting antibiotics,' affirming the multi-antibiotic response.

results.result: Different antibiotics cause ribosomes to stall at different positions within toiL: tetracycline and retapamulin stall at the start codon, tylosin stalls at Val5, and erythromycin stalls during translation termination. Ribosome stalling at various positions within toiL is sufficient to induce topAI expression, making toiL a multipurpose uORF.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe this as convincing evidence using multiple approaches. The editor highlights 'a creative approach to map the different locations of ribosome stalling within toiL induced by different antibiotics' as a strength. One reviewer notes 'the authors used multiple different approaches such as...ribosome profiling to examine the consequences of various antibiotics on toiL-mediated regulation,' affirming the stalling position data.

results.result: SHAPE-seq analysis reveals that the topAI upstream region forms a secondary structure where sequences within toiL base-pair with the topAI ribosome-binding site. Upon tetracycline treatment, the toiL region becomes less reactive (more structured) while the topAI Shine-Dalgarno sequence becomes more reactive (less structured), consistent with ribosome stalling disrupting the repressive hairpin.
results.evaluation: One reviewer explicitly states 'the authors have satisfactorily addressed all major concerns raised by the reviewers, particularly regarding the SHAPE-seq data,' indicating that initial concerns were resolved. The editor notes the study combines approaches 'with ribosome profiling and RNA structure probing by SHAPE' as a strength, affirming acceptance of these structural data.

results.result: ChIP-qPCR and qRT-PCR experiments demonstrate that mutation of rho or treatment with tetracycline increases RNAP occupancy and RNA levels across the topAI-yjhQP operon. Tetracycline treatment inhibits Rho-dependent transcription termination within topAI by inducing translation of topAI.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the overall model as supported by 'convincing data' and 'several of the experimental data mainly support it.' The ChIP-qPCR and qRT-PCR data are part of the multiple approaches reviewers cite as strengths, with no specific criticisms of these experiments raised in the reviews.

results.result: The authors propose a regulatory model where, under normal conditions, a hairpin encompassing toiL and the topAI ribosome-binding site prevents topAI translation, promoting Rho termination. Upon translation stress, ribosomes stall within toiL, disrupting the hairpin and allowing topAI translation, which prevents Rho termination. The ability of toiL to respond to diverse stresses is due to base-pairing across the entire toiL ORF length.
results.evaluation: Multiple reviewers describe the model as 'appealing' and 'elegant' with 'convincing data' supporting it. One reviewer states 'the authors provide convincing data to support an elegant model in which ribosome stalling by ToiL promotes downstream topAI translation and prevents premature Rho-dependent transcription termination.' Another notes 'the model is appealing and several of the experimental data mainly support it.'

results.result: Mutations in 23S rRNA (helix 69 and helix 80) that affect ribosome processivity induce topAI expression. A mutant 23S rRNA supplied in trans is dominant over wild-type chromosomal copies, suggesting the effect is not simply due to reduced ribosome levels but rather altered ribosome function.
results.evaluation: The editor specifically highlights 'a genetic screen to identify 23S rRNA mutations that affect topA1 expression' as a strength of the study. Reviewers note the use of 'multiple different approaches such as a genetic screen to identify factors such as 23S rRNA mutations' without raising concerns about these findings.

results.result: The Rut for topAI is located within the 5' upstream region rather than within the ORF itself, which is distinct from other characterized examples of Rho-terminated genes. The Rut must overlap toiL and remains functional despite the presence of an actively translated overlapping ORF. Ribosomes translating topAI likely prevent Rho from catching elongating RNAP rather than preventing Rho loading.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the mechanistic model without challenging the location or function of the Rut. The overall regulatory mechanism is described as supported by 'convincing data' and the model as 'elegant,' implicitly accepting these mechanistic details about Rut location and function.

results.result: The authors speculate that topAI and/or yjhQ/P may have additional functions beyond the characterized DNA gyrase inhibitor activity, potentially linked to sensing of ribosome-targeting antibiotics or non-antibiotic molecules such as amino acids or polyamines.
results.evaluation: Multiple reviewers explicitly note this as an unresolved question. The editor states 'the work leaves unanswered how bacteria benefit by activating expression of the genes using the proposed strategy.' Two reviewers note 'it remains unanswered...what is the physiological role of the induced expression of the topAI/yjhQ/yjhP operon' and 'the physiological consequences of activating topAI-yjhQP expression upon exposure to various ribosome-targeting antibiotics remain unresolved.'

results.result: The authors speculate that the toiL sequence has evolved to stall ribosomes in a sequence-specific manner in response to a variety of antibiotics, explaining its ability to sense multiple structurally distinct compounds.
results.evaluation: The editor explicitly states 'the work leaves unanswered...the mechanism underlying ToiL's sensing of structurally distinct antibiotics.' One reviewer notes 'future experiments will be needed to...elucidate the mechanism of specific antibiotic sensing,' indicating this mechanistic speculation is not yet resolved.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on toiL identification and characterization (C4, C32, C33, C49, C50, C51, C52). Both evaluations find the evidence convincing, with OpenEval highlighting converging experimental evidence from ribosome profiling, reporter assays, and sequence conservation, while peer reviewers describe this as a key discovery with convincing evidence.

Perfect agreement on Rut location and mechanism (C139, C140, C141, C144, C145). Both evaluations support these claims about the unusual Rut location in the 5' UR and its overlap with toiL, with OpenEval finding the inference logical and peer reviewers implicitly accepting these mechanistic details as part of the elegant model.

Strong agreement on Rho-dependent termination mechanism (C31, C37-C43, C45-C47). Both evaluations find the reporter assays, ChIP-qPCR, and mutational analysis convincing. OpenEval emphasizes multiple lines of experimental evidence while peer reviewers describe the model as elegant and supported by convincing data. Peer review also includes C5 and C6 which OpenEval addresses separately.

Strong agreement on multi-antibiotic response (C7, C61, C62, C65, C66). Both evaluations accept the luciferase reporter data showing diverse translation stress responses. OpenEval highlights the requirement for toiL translation demonstrated by mutations (C53, C54), while peer reviewers accept the finding without criticism and note the creative approach.

Strong agreement on antibiotic-specific stalling positions (C8, C85, C86, C87, C91-C94, C97, C98, C115). Both evaluations find the ribosome profiling and stalling reporter data convincing. OpenEval notes spectinomycin data are less clear (C95), while peer reviewers highlight the creative mapping approach as a strength. OpenEval also includes C83, C84 not in peer review.

Strong agreement on RNA secondary structure (C77, C79, C80, C81, C82). Both evaluations support the structural model. OpenEval emphasizes multiple independent lines of evidence including computational prediction, evolutionary conservation, and SHAPE-seq validation. Peer reviewers note initial concerns were satisfactorily addressed, particularly regarding SHAPE-seq data. OpenEval also includes C5, C78, C99, C100 not in peer review.

Strong agreement on trans-complementation and rRNA mutations (C56, C57, C58). Both evaluations support the genetic screen findings. OpenEval notes the dominance observation is reasonable but mechanism not fully explained, while peer reviewers highlight the genetic screen as a specific strength. OpenEval also addresses C108 (ribosome processivity) which peer review includes separately.

Agreement on overall regulatory model with partial claim overlap (C71, C72, C75, C76). Both evaluations support the integration of ChIP-qPCR and qRT-PCR data. OpenEval emphasizes internal consistency of the mechanistic model, while peer reviewers describe it as supported by convincing data. Peer review includes additional claims (C67-C70, C73, C74) that OpenEval addresses in other results.

Agreement on position-independent regulation mechanism (C9, C106, C107). Both evaluations support this conclusion. OpenEval finds it well-supported by structural data, stalling reporters, and mutational analysis, describing the mechanistic explanation as logical. Peer reviewers describe the overall model as elegant and appealing with convincing data. Peer review also includes C99, C100, C102, C103 addressed elsewhere by OpenEval.

Agreement on uncertainty regarding physiological role (C152, C153). Both evaluations mark this as uncertain/unresolved. OpenEval notes these are speculative claims extending beyond experimental data, while peer reviewers explicitly state this remains an unanswered question about how bacteria benefit from this regulatory strategy. OpenEval also includes C110, C156 which peer review addresses separately.

Agreement on ribosome processivity mechanism (C108). Both evaluations support this explanation. OpenEval finds it consistent with genetic screen results and trans-complementation data, supported by citations to prior work. Peer reviewers accept the genetic screen findings without raising concerns. This claim appears in different groupings in each evaluation.

Agreement on uncertainty regarding antibiotic sensing mechanism (C110). Both evaluations mark this as uncertain/speculative. OpenEval notes this is speculation without direct experimental support, while peer reviewers explicitly state the mechanism underlying ToiL's sensing of structurally distinct antibiotics remains unanswered and requires future experiments.

OpenEval evaluates mRNA stability regulation (C104, C105) as uncertain, noting the 2-fold increase could reflect multiple mechanisms and requires additional experiments like RNA half-life measurements. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific claims.

OpenEval supports the inference about RNA destabilization in rho mutants (C74) based on qRT-PCR data showing increased RNA levels upstream of termination site. While peer review R6 includes C74, it groups it with other claims and doesn't specifically evaluate this destabilization inference.

OpenEval supports the broader implication about widespread uORF-mediated antibiotic sensing (C157) based on ribosome profiling analysis of other known uORF-containing genes, though notes functional validation would strengthen the conclusion. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval supports the mechanistic explanations for antibiotic-specific stalling (C120, C121, C123-C136), finding them well-supported by citations to prior work and consistent with experimental observations. The chloramphenicol explanation is noted as speculative but reasonable. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval evaluates background claims about topoisomerases and DNA topology (C1-C3, C10-C26) as supported by appropriate citations, representing established knowledge providing necessary context. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.

OpenEval evaluates prior work on topAI regulation and related systems (C27-C30, C34-C35, C59-C60, C63-C64) as supported by appropriate citations, establishing what was known before this study. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.

OpenEval supports comparisons to other regulatory systems (C111-C114, C116-C119), finding them accurately represent prior work with appropriate citations. The distinction between toiL and other systems (C115) is well-supported by experimental data. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval evaluates proposed mechanisms for Rho function (C146, C147, C148) as uncertain, noting these are speculative proposals without direct experimental support in the study. While citation to prior work provides precedent, neither mechanism is tested experimentally. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
